scenario: AITA For refusing to sit next to a kid with autism during a lecture, and sitting on the floor instead? | I know this sounds bad but bare with me, I’m (23m) in a class that has exactly 30 seats, and there are 31 students. I was running late and walked in a minute before the lecture began. There was only one open seat. I walked over to it and in the next seat over sitting was a kid with autism, he is very socially inept but totally brilliant. The problem is that he smelled like he hadn’t showered in a few weeks, his hair was greasier than Snapes, and he was wearing stained pajamas. I sat next to him for 2 minutes before I was about to gag and I got up and sat on the floor in the back of the lecture hall. The professor saw this and asked if I moved because of the smell, he asked in front of the whole class, I said I just didn’t want to sit there and he continued lecturing. After class a few of the kids said I was TA because I should have just sucked it up for the hour and dealt with the smell. So Reddit AITA?

prediction.raw: I would rate this as 1, meaning YTA (You're The Asshole). While it's understandable that the smell and appearance of the student with autism might be uncomfortable, refusing to sit next to him and instead sitting on the floor can be perceived as rude and discriminatory. The student with autism may not have the same ability to understand or control his personal hygiene, and it's not his fault if he has difficulty with social interactions or personal care. By getting up and moving, the original poster (OP) drew attention to the situation and potentially embarrassed the student with autism. It would have been more considerate to either sit in the available seat and try to tolerate the smell for the duration of the lecture or to discreetly ask the professor if there were any alternative seating arrangements. Additionally, the OP's decision to move was not only about his own discomfort but also about avoiding the student with autism, which can be seen as ableist and stigmatizing. The fact that the OP mentioned the student's autism and social ineptness in the context of explaining why he didn't want to sit next to him suggests that he was making assumptions or judgments about the student based on his disability. It's worth noting that the OP's actions may have been perceived as hurtful or alienating by the student with autism and possibly by others in the class who may have autism or other disabilities. A more empathetic and inclusive approach would have been to try to understand and accommodate the student's needs, rather than avoiding him due to personal discomfort.
